topics.title: How to add an AI agent to an existing Next.js app—with streaming, auth, and persistent sessions
topics.description: Embed a file-defined agent in an existing Next.js application while keeping the application's authentication, database, routes, and deployment boundaries.
topics.audience: TypeScript product developers adding an agent as one feature inside an existing Next.js application.
topics.outcome: A runnable support-agent route that authenticates the caller, maps the user to a stable session, streams SSE, and calls an existing typed database tool without introducing a second backend.
requiredSections: Mount the agent behind a Route Handler
Use the existing database through a typed tool
Deploy with the right state model
When not to use this shape
boundaries: The application owns authentication and authorization; FastAgent does not infer either.
The default JSONL session store is a single-process tier.
Do not present Vercel's stateless function tier as an out-of-the-box durable FastAgent deployment.
Use Node.js 22.19 or newer and state storage appropriate to the host.

topics.title: Build a self-hosted GitHub pull request review agent with FastAgent
topics.description: Turn verified GitHub webhook events into focused pull request reviews using a file-defined agent you can run and inspect yourself.
topics.audience: Developers who want a review agent attached to their own repository without adopting a hosted agent platform.
topics.outcome: A reproducible review agent that verifies webhook signatures, selects pull request events, posts a useful review, and states the post-ack durability boundary honestly.
requiredSections: Define what the reviewer should do
When not to use an agent reviewer
boundaries: GitHub webhook turns are acknowledged before background agent work finishes.
The shipped GitHub channel has no durable post-ack replay.
Do not claim exactly-once review execution.
A reviewer should be advisory and must not silently become a merge authority.

topics.title: Give an AI agent a clock: cron, wake, and self-scheduling without a workflow DSL
topics.description: Use static schedules for known jobs and persisted wake-ups for agent-chosen follow-ups, with clear delivery and retry semantics.
topics.audience: Agent developers who need periodic work or delayed follow-ups but do not need a deterministic workflow engine.
topics.outcome: A practical explanation and working example of static cron, wake/unwake, schedule history, delivery tools, and host-specific clock behavior.
requiredSections: Deliver the result through a tool
Let the agent schedule its own follow-up
How clocks map to deployment targets
When to use a workflow engine instead
boundaries: A schedule invokes the agent; delivery still belongs to an explicit tool.
Resident deployments need a running process for local cron and wake timers.
AgentCore maps supported clocks to EventBridge only for the shared ingress surface.
FastAgent is not a deterministic workflow engine.

topics.title: Group-chat agents should behave like participants, not endpoints
topics.description: Derive when an agent should speak, where it should answer, and what it should remember from the social structure of the room.
topics.audience: Developers designing Slack, Feishu, Lark, or Telegram agents for real group conversations.
topics.outcome: A platform-neutral design argument backed by concrete Slack, Feishu/Lark, and Telegram behavior.
requiredSections: Why the place is the concurrency unit
How the rule maps to Slack, Feishu, and Telegram
The cost of weaker platform signals
boundaries: Do not claim complete knowledge of thread membership when the platform only provides observed events.
Do not describe one platform's placement rule as universal.
Group context permissions and least-privilege mention-only modes must both be stated.
Sessions follow conversation places, not individual users in a room.

topics.title: Turn an agent directory into a Feishu or Lark teammate
topics.description: Connect a file-defined agent to Feishu or Lark with explicit permissions, thread behavior, streaming cards, durable turn intent, and a deployable webhook path.
topics.audience: Teams that want an agent in Feishu or Lark and need a realistic setup path beyond a toy echo bot.
topics.outcome: An end-to-end onboarding and deployment tutorial that explains transport choice, permissions, publication steps, room memory, and operational limits.
requiredSections: Test direct messages, rooms, and threads
boundaries: Onboarding includes human confirmation and application publication steps.
WebSocket is a long-connection channel and requires always-on compute.
Context-aware group behavior requests broader message visibility than mention-only mode.
Accepted turns replay at least once; exactly-once side effects are not guaranteed.

topics.title: What reliable agent serving actually means: ACKs, leases, replay, and failure windows
topics.description: A precise guide to the reliability guarantees that sit between an accepted webhook and a completed agent turn.
topics.audience: Senior developers evaluating whether an agent serving layer is ready for production workloads.
topics.outcome: A concrete reliability vocabulary and channel-by-channel matrix that separates acceptance, execution, delivery, and recovery.
requiredSections: Split the delivery path into stages
Why one session needs one writer
How deployment changes the failure window
When you need a workflow or queue above FastAgent
boundaries: Do not claim universal exactly-once execution.
GitHub post-ack work and replaying chat channels have different guarantees.
A repaired transcript does not make tool side effects exactly once.
Multi-instance durability requires external backends above the shipped file tier.
